title: Transactional Outbox & Change Data Capture
summary: Propagate committed database changes to queues, caches, and search indexes without dual-write drift.
body:
Updating a primary database and publishing to Kafka or invalidating a search index in application code creates a dual-write race: a crash, timeout, or rollback between the two leaves downstream state permanently out of sync.

## Transactional outbox + relay
Keep the database transaction as the single atomic commit point:
- Write the domain row mutation and an `outbox_events` row (`event_id`, `aggregate_id`, `event_type`, `payload`, `created_at`) inside the same local ACID transaction.
- Have an asynchronous relay poll unpublished rows (or tail the database write-ahead log) and publish to the broker, marking rows published only after broker acknowledgement.
- Because the relay can crash after broker ack and before marking the row, delivery is `at-least-once`: every downstream consumer must deduplicate by `event_id`.

## Log-based Change Data Capture (CDC)
When deriving read models across tables (full-text search, analytics warehouses, cache invalidation), tail the database transaction log (`WAL` or `binlog`) with a connector such as Debezium:
- Zero application dual writes and minimal OLTP overhead compared with heavy polling queries.
- Ordering is preserved per partition key (typically `tenant_id` or `aggregate_id`), not globally across partitions.
- Watch out for schema coupling: streaming raw internal table columns turns private schema refactors into breaking public contract changes. Prefer streaming an explicit `outbox` table when crossing team boundaries.

## Failure modes to address
- Replication-slot disk growth: if PostgreSQL logical replication slots stall while a connector is down, `WAL` segments accumulate and can fill primary disk unless slot lag alerts and retention caps are configured.
- Cold rebuilds and drift: design derived search/cache projections so you can snapshot-backfill from the source of truth and replay from a known log offset.
